statements.status_notes: GHSA-72hv-8253-57qq is a missing maxNumberLength validation in jackson-core's non-blocking (async) parser (NonBlockingUtf8JsonParserBase skips the resetInt()/resetFloat() length checks), fixed in jackson-core 2.21.1. The 2.19.2 copy Scout flags in this image is not the classpath jackson-core: upstream DataHub v1.5.0.7 pins jacksonVersion 2.21.3, and the fat jar's BOOT-INF/lib carries jackson-core-2.21.3.jar, which already contains the fix. The 2.19.2 copy exists only as classes relocated to com.hazelcast.shaded.com.fasterxml.jackson.core inside hazelcast-5.6.0.jar (identified via its bundled pom.properties), where Gradle's resolutionStrategy cannot reach it. Verified against the built mce-consumer-job.jar: a byte-level scan of every class in the fat jar and all 576 bundled libraries found zero classes referencing com/hazelcast/shaded/com/fasterxml/jackson/core/json/async, and no Hazelcast class invokes createNonBlockingByteArrayParser or createNonBlockingParser on the relocated copy, so the vulnerable async parser in the 2.19.2 copy has no call sites. The async call sites that do exist (rest.li entitystream decoders, vertx JsonParserImpl, spring-web Jackson2Tokenizer) bind to the fixed 2.21.3 classpath copy, and AWS SDK's third-party-jackson-core 2.32.25 is a separately versioned artifact. The shaded fix lands with Hazelcast 5.7.0 (bundles jackson-core 2.21.2); a 5.6 to 5.7 Hazelcast bump is upstream-managed and out of scope for a CVE remediation. This basis must be revisited if a future DataHub release starts feeding data through Hazelcast's relocated async parser.

jackson-core 2.19.4 and 2.19.0 are bundled in the upstream dhi/kafka image at /opt/kafka/libs/. Multiple attempts to override these versions via cruise-control and third-party Maven dependency patches have not succeeded in replacing the Kafka-bundled JARs. The fixed version 2.21.1 is specified in cruise-control-mvn-deps.json but does not affect the jackson-core artifacts shipped with Kafka itself. A complete fix requires either: (1) updating jackson-core in the upstream dhi/kafka image, or (2) implementing a build step in strimzi-kafka to remove the old jackson-core JARs from /opt/kafka/libs/ and replace them with 2.21.1. Tracking upstream kafka image updates and evaluating JAR replacement strategies.

GHSA-72hv-8253-57qq is missing integer length validation in jackson-core's async parser (NonBlockingUtf8JsonParserBase._valueComplete). The 2.19.2 copy is brought in by Spring Boot 3.5.x's transitive BOM after DataHub v1.5.0.7's upstream spring-boot bump from 3.4.x to 3.5.14; it is separate from the 2.15.2 copy addressed in the earlier statement (which is shaded inside Hazelcast). The async-parser code path is unreachable for the same reason as before: DataHub's mae-consumer has no NonBlockingJsonParser or createNonBlockingByteArrayParser call sites. The fix lands in jackson-core 2.21.1+; awaiting a Spring Boot patch release that picks that up in its BOM.

GHSA-72hv-8253-57qq is missing integer length validation in jackson-core's async parser (NonBlockingUtf8JsonParserBase._valueComplete). The 2.19.2 copy is shaded inside Hazelcast (e.g. hazelcast-5.6.0.jar under BOOT-INF/lib) and is unreachable by Gradle resolutionStrategy or force-cve-deps.gradle. The async-parser code path is unreachable: DataHub GMS has no NonBlockingJsonParser or createNonBlockingByteArrayParser call sites. Unshaded jackson-core copies in the WAR are forced to 2.21.1+ during the image build.

Jackson Core 2.19.2 is embedded in parquet-hadoop-bundle-1.17.0.jar (shaded dependency in esql-datasource-iceberg and esql-datasource-parquet modules), and Jackson Core 2.17.2 is embedded in elasticsearch-x-content-9.4.1.jar. These are shaded/relocated dependencies that cannot be bumped via Gradle resolutionStrategy. Fixing requires either upstream Elasticsearch to rebuild these modules with patched Jackson versions, or bumping to parquet-hadoop-bundle versions that embed fixed Jackson (if available). The vulnerability allows unbounded memory allocation via crafted JSON, but Elasticsearch's typical deployment behind reverse proxies with request size limits provides some mitigation.
